funFacts.text: Huntsville is nicknamed "Rocket City" — the Saturn V rocket that carried astronauts to the Moon was developed there.
Montgomery was the first capital of the Confederacy, in 1861.
The Montgomery bus boycott began in 1955 after Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat.
Alaska has more coastline than all the other U.S. states combined.
The United States bought Alaska from Russia in 1867 for $7.2 million.
Denali, at 20,310 feet, is the tallest mountain in North America.
Most of Arizona doesn't change its clocks for daylight saving time.
Arizona was the last of the 48 contiguous states to join the Union, on February 14, 1912.
The Grand Canyon is about 277 miles long and more than a mile deep.
At Crater of Diamonds State Park, visitors can dig for real diamonds and keep what they find.
Hot Springs was set aside by Congress in 1832, before the idea of a national park even existed.
Walmart opened its first store in Rogers, Arkansas, in 1962.
Death Valley holds the record for the hottest air temperature ever measured on Earth: 134 °F, in 1913.
Mount Whitney, at 14,505 feet, is the highest point in the contiguous United States.
The discovery of gold at Sutter's Mill in 1848 set off the California Gold Rush.
Colorado's borders are made only of lines of latitude and longitude — one of just three states like that, with Utah and Wyoming.
Denver is the "Mile High City" — its official elevation is exactly one mile (5,280 feet).
Colorado is the only U.S. state that lies entirely above 1,000 meters (about 3,300 feet) of elevation.
Connecticut is nicknamed the Constitution State for its Fundamental Orders of 1639, often called the first written constitution in America.
USS Nautilus, the world's first nuclear-powered submarine, was built in Groton, Connecticut.
Yale University in New Haven was founded in 1701.
Delaware was the first state to ratify the U.S. Constitution, on December 7, 1787.
Delaware is the second-smallest state by area, after Rhode Island.
Delaware's curved northern border with Pennsylvania is called the Twelve-Mile Circle.
Florida has the longest coastline in the contiguous United States.
St. Augustine, founded in 1565, is the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the continental U.S.
Everglades National Park is home to both American alligators and American crocodiles.
Georgia was the fourth state to ratify the U.S. Constitution, on January 2, 1788.
Coca-Cola was invented in Atlanta in 1886.
Martin Luther King Jr. was born in Atlanta in 1929.
Hawaii is the only U.S. state that is an archipelago — a chain of islands.
Hawaii's state constitution names two official languages: English and Hawaiian.
Measured from its base on the ocean floor, Mauna Kea is taller than Mount Everest.
Hells Canyon, on the Idaho–Oregon border, is North America's deepest river gorge — deeper than the Grand Canyon.
Shoshone Falls on the Snake River is taller than Niagara Falls.
Idaho is nicknamed the Gem State: 72 kinds of precious and semi-precious stones are found there.
When it was finished in 1973, Chicago's Willis Tower (then the Sears Tower) was the tallest building in the world.
Abraham Lincoln is buried in Springfield, Illinois.
In 1900, engineers reversed the Chicago River so it flows away from Lake Michigan.
The Indianapolis 500 race was first run in 1911.
The Indianapolis Motor Speedway has the largest seating capacity of any sports venue in the world.
No one knows for sure where the word "Hoosier" comes from — historians still debate it.
Iowa is the only state whose east and west borders are formed almost entirely by rivers — the Mississippi on the east, and the Missouri and Big Sioux on the west.
The baseball field from the movie Field of Dreams is in Dyersville, Iowa.
The Iowa State Capitol is the only state capitol in the country with five domes.
The geographic center of the 48 contiguous states is near Lebanon, Kansas.
Dorothy's story in The Wonderful Wizard of Oz begins on a farm in Kansas.
Monument Rocks was the first place in Kansas to be named a National Natural Landmark by the U.S. Department of the Interior.
The Kentucky Derby, traditionally held in May at Churchill Downs, has been run every year since 1875.
Mammoth Cave is the longest known cave system in the world.
Both Abraham Lincoln and Confederate president Jefferson Davis were born in Kentucky.
Louisiana is divided into parishes instead of counties.
Jazz was born in the African-American communities of New Orleans in the late 1800s and early 1900s.
The Lake Pontchartrain Causeway, nearly 24 miles long, holds the Guinness World Record for the longest continuous bridge over water.
Maine is the only state that borders just one other state: New Hampshire.
Maine is the northernmost and largest state in New England — almost half of the region's land area.
Maine is the largest producer of lobster in the United States.
"The Star-Spangled Banner" was written after the British bombarded Fort McHenry in Baltimore in 1814.
Chesapeake Bay is the largest estuary in the United States.
Maryland gave land to create Washington, D.C.
The Pilgrims arrived on the Mayflower and founded Plymouth Colony in 1620.
Harvard, founded in 1636, is the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States.
Basketball was invented in Springfield, Massachusetts, by James Naismith in 1891.
Michigan is made of two peninsulas, and no point in the state is more than 85 miles from one of the Great Lakes.
Michigan touches four of the five Great Lakes.
The Mackinac Bridge, nearly 5 miles long, connects Michigan's Upper and Lower Peninsulas.
Minnesota is called the "Land of 10,000 Lakes" — and it actually has more than 11,000.
The Mississippi River begins at Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota.
Minnesota's Northwest Angle is the northernmost point of the contiguous United States.
The Mississippi River forms most of Mississippi's western border.
Elvis Presley was born in Tupelo, Mississippi, in 1935.
Barq's root beer comes from Biloxi, Mississippi, where Edward Barq opened the Biloxi Artesian Bottling Works in the late 1890s.
St. Louis's Gateway Arch, at 630 feet, is the tallest arch in the world.
Missouri borders eight other states — tied with Tennessee for the most.
Mark Twain grew up in Hannibal, Missouri, the town that inspired Tom Sawyer's hometown.
Montana's name comes from the Spanish word montaña, meaning "mountain."
In 1932, Glacier National Park and Canada's Waterton Lakes National Park were joined as the Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park.
The Battle of the Little Bighorn — "Custer's Last Stand" — was fought in Montana in 1876.
Nebraska is the only state with a one-house (unicameral) legislature. Voters approved it in 1934, and it first met in 1937.
Arbor Day was first celebrated in Nebraska in 1872.
Chimney Rock was a famous landmark for pioneers on the Oregon Trail.
Nevada is the driest state in the United States.
Hoover Dam, on the Nevada–Arizona border, was finished in 1936 and created Lake Mead.
Nevada joined the Union during the Civil War, which is why it's called the "Battle Born State."
New Hampshire's state motto is "Live Free or Die."
Mount Washington recorded a 231 mph wind gust in 1934, a world record for 62 years.
New Hampshire has the shortest ocean coastline of any coastal U.S. state — about 18 miles.
New Jersey is the most densely populated U.S. state.
Thomas Edison developed the phonograph and a practical light bulb at his lab in Menlo Park, New Jersey.
On June 19, 1846, Hoboken, New Jersey, hosted what is considered the first fully documented baseball game.
Santa Fe, founded in 1610, is the oldest state capital city in the U.S.
Santa Fe is also the highest state capital, at about 7,200 feet above sea level.
Carlsbad Caverns National Park protects more than 119 caves.
New York City was the capital of the United States from 1785 until 1790.
The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France, dedicated in 1886.
Niagara Falls sits on New York's border with Canada.
The Wright brothers made the first controlled, powered airplane flight near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903.
Mount Mitchell is the highest peak east of the Mississippi River.
The Cape Hatteras Lighthouse is the tallest brick lighthouse in the United States.
Rugby, North Dakota, claims to be the geographic center of North America.
Theodore Roosevelt ranched in North Dakota's badlands in the 1880s; the national park there is named for him.
The International Peace Garden straddles North Dakota's border with Canada.
Seven U.S. presidents were born in Ohio.
Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the Moon, grew up near Wapakoneta, Ohio.
Ohio's flag is the only U.S. state flag that isn't a rectangle.
The name Oklahoma comes from Choctaw words meaning "red people."
In the Land Run of 1889, settlers raced to claim land on a single day: April 22.
The Oklahoma Panhandle was once known as "No Man's Land."
Crater Lake, at 1,949 feet, is the deepest lake in the United States.
Oregon's flag is the only U.S. state flag with a different design on each side.
Portland's Mill Ends Park was named the world's smallest park by Guinness World Records.
Both the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution were signed at Independence Hall in Philadelphia.
Hershey, Pennsylvania, was founded in 1903 as a town for the workers of Milton S. Hershey's chocolate company.
The Battle of Gettysburg, a turning point of the Civil War, was fought in Pennsylvania in 1863.
Rhode Island is the smallest U.S. state by area.
Rhode Island was the first colony to renounce its allegiance to the British Crown, on May 4, 1776.
The first U.S. Open golf championship was played in Newport, Rhode Island, in 1895.
The Civil War began with the attack on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor in April 1861.
South Carolina was the first state to secede from the Union, in December 1860.
Charleston's Rainbow Row is 13 historic houses named for the pastel colors they were painted when restored in the 1930s and 1940s.
Each president's head on Mount Rushmore is 60 feet tall.
The Crazy Horse Memorial in the Black Hills has been under construction since 1948.
Pierre is one of only four state capitals not served by an Interstate highway.
Tennessee borders eight other states — tied with Missouri for the most.
Great Smoky Mountains, shared with North Carolina, is the most visited national park in the U.S.
Nashville is known as "Music City" and is home to the Grand Ole Opry.
Texas was an independent country, the Republic of Texas, from 1836 to 1845.
Texas is the largest state in the contiguous United States.
NASA's Mission Control for human spaceflight is at Johnson Space Center in Houston.
The Great Salt Lake is the largest saltwater lake in the Western Hemisphere.
The first transcontinental railroad was completed at Promontory Summit, Utah, in 1869.
Utah has five national parks — Arches, Bryce Canyon, Canyonlands, Capitol Reef and Zion — the third most of any state.
Vermont produces more maple syrup than any other U.S. state.
Montpelier is the least populous state capital in the United States.
Vermont was an independent republic from 1777 to 1791 before becoming the 14th state.
Eight U.S. presidents were born in Virginia — more than in any other state.
Jamestown, founded in 1607, was the first permanent English settlement in the Americas.
The Pentagon, in Arlington, is one of the world's largest office buildings.
Washington is the only U.S. state named after a president.
The 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens was the deadliest and most destructive volcanic eruption in the history of the contiguous U.S.
Seattle's Space Needle was built for the 1962 World's Fair.
West Virginia is the only state that lies entirely within the region known as Appalachia.
West Virginia split from Virginia during the Civil War and became a state in 1863.
When it opened in 1977, the New River Gorge Bridge was the world's longest single-span arch bridge.
Wisconsin is known as "America's Dairyland" and is famous for its cheese.
The first kindergarten in the United States opened in Watertown, Wisconsin, in 1856.
The Green Bay Packers are the only community-owned team in North America's four major professional sports leagues.
Yellowstone, mostly in Wyoming, became the world's first national park in 1872.
In 1869, Wyoming became the first U.S. territory to give women the right to vote.
Devils Tower became the first U.S. national monument in 1906.
